Review whether any issues or concerns were raised at previous disclosure opportunities regarding comprehension of information on modern slavery and human trafficking, or whether any issues or concerns were raised at the time regarding their willingness or ability to disclose.

14.17. If an individual was informed of their rights relating to modern slavery, had opportunities to disclose information in a safe environment, and fails to do so (particularly where there have been multiple failures to do so), the decision maker should take these factors into account when assessing the credibility of an individual’s version of events when it is provided. For example, a situation where:

An individual has been issued guidance on modern slavery and human trafficking;

They have been given multiple opportunities to share information relevant to or that could form the basis of an NRM referral;

They have not done so; and

At a later stage, for example, once Home Office removal action against the person is underway, or close to a hearing date for a criminal case, they make a disclosure indicating they may have been exploited.

14.18. In circumstances such as these, decision makers should take the timing of the disclosure into account as part of their credibility assessment.

14.19. Where the timing of disclosure is such that it is considered to undermine an individual’s credibility and there is no sufficient explanation or contrary evidence to offset this, the decision maker should consider this as part of their credibility assessment and may issue a negative RG decision on the grounds of credibility.

Reasons for delayed disclosure

14.20. When assessing reasons for delayed disclosure, the following principles apply:

Trauma, incomprehension of information provided on modern slavery and human trafficking or other reasons for delay should not be presumed. This must be documented at the time and supported by professional insight, such as by the first responder or medical expert.

If an individual provides an explanation for delayed disclosure (such as being impacted by trauma, fear of authorities, cultural or gender-based barriers, or lack of self-identification as a victim), this can be factored into a decision maker’s assessment of credibility if that reason is a credible, evidenced explanation, such as one supported by a credible, evidenced explanation, for example, an explanation supported by the professional judgement of a First Responder or relevant medical expert.

Decision makers must consider all relevant available information when assessing reasons provided for delayed disclosure. When reviewing this information, decision makers should:

Examine what information was disclosed, when, to whom, and in what circumstances.

Assess whether the individual disclosed information to First Responders or other authorities at an earlier stage than in their NRM account, or whether the information provided in the NRM account represents new information not previously disclosed.

Consider the nature and basis of the information shared, and whether this information indicates that the reasons for delayed disclosure are credible.

Decision makers must not issue a negative decision based on late disclosure if the individual did not have opportunities to disclose, or if concerns about comprehension, support, or safety were raised at the time of the disclosure opportunity and not addressed.

Assessing timing of disclosure in children

14.21. In cases involving individuals under 18 at the point of referral, decision makers must assess the timing of disclosure in view of specific factors relevant to the response of children to exploitation, and the impact that may have on their disclosure of relevant information. Where available, these factors include: the child’s developmental stage and maturity, their cognitive and emotional capacity, background and personal circumstances, the nature and duration of the exploitation experienced, evidence of trauma suffered, and any possible enduring impact of grooming, coercion, or control by exploiters.

14.22. Decision makers must also recognise that children may be unable to identify safe opportunities to disclose, may not recognise their experiences as exploitation, or may be unwilling or unable to speak due to mistrust of authority figures.

14.23. Where these factors are present, the expectation is that the child will be excluded from any adverse credibility finding based on the timing of their disclosure. This position should only be departed from where the decision maker identifies compelling reasons as to why it would be appropriate to do so.

Considering gender and culture

14.24. All competent authority staff need to know how to consider gender and cultural issues in considering credibility.

14.25. It is important to understand that distress presents differently in different cultures and that cultural understanding of many situations is variable.

14.26. When making Reasonable Grounds and Conclusive Grounds decisions competent authorities must take into account the individual position and personal circumstances of the person and consider culture and gender issues.

14.27. Men and women from the same country of origin may have different experiences due to their cultural, ethnic, gender and sexual identity. For example, women may be unable to disclose relevant details due to cultural and social norms.

Relevance of potential prosecution of exploiters

14.28. All staff need to know about how prosecution of their exploiters could impact a victim of modern slavery’s Reasonable Grounds and Conclusive Grounds decisions.

15.141. Where appropriate to victims of modern slavery, work coaches can use the Domestic Emergency provision to “switch off” work related requirements for a period of up to a month at a time. Consideration to individual needs is paramount and work coaches will need to be flexible and ensure that requirements that are set are reasonable in light of the claimant’s circumstances.

15.142. Where there are other circumstances that would prevent a person from working such as a health condition, disability or attending court as a witness or defendant, work related activities can be tailored.

Access to legal representation

15.143. Any victim of modern slavery can appoint their own legal representative where they can afford to do so. It is advised to use a solicitor registered with or regulated by an officially accredited body such as the Law Society, Solicitors Regulation Authority or the Office of the Immigration Services Commissioner (OISC).

15.144. If a victim cannot afford a legal representative, they may be eligible for legal aid (see below) or they can try and find a pro bono legal representative. As with paid representatives, it is advised to use a solicitor regulated with an officially accredited body.

Access to legal aid

15.145. Information in this section refers to legal aid in England and Wales. Information regarding legal aid in Scotland is available here.

Criminal legal aid

15.146. Victims can receive legally aided representation in criminal proceedings against them.

Civil legal aid

15.147. All potential victims or victims of modern slavery can apply for legal aid for all civil legal services listed in Schedule 1, Part 1 of the Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012 (LASPO).

15.148. These civil legal services are available to adults and children. Further information on civil legal aid for children can be found at paragraph 16.62.

15.149. All applicants for legal aid must meet the relevant statutory criteria, which includes means and merits tests.

15.150. Victims and support providers can check the eligibility to access civil legal aid here.

Legal aid for victims of modern slavery

15.151. Section 47 of the Modern Slavery Act 2015 amended the Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders (LASPO) Act 2012 to allow victims of ‘slavery, servitude and forced or compulsory labour’ to apply for legal aid for the same types of cases as human trafficking victims.

15.152. These civil legal services are accessible to potential victims and victims of modern slavery with a positive Reasonable Grounds decision or a positive Conclusive Grounds decision.

15.153. These civil legal services are also subject to the statutory criteria of means and merits tests.

Legal aid for immigration advice on permission to stay

15.154. Potential victims or victims of modern slavery with a positive Reasonable Grounds or a positive Conclusive Grounds decision can access legal aid for advice on an application for permission to stay.

Legal aid for advice on an asylum claim

15.155. Potential victims and victims of modern slavery may apply for legal aid in relation to an asylum claim at any point. Legal aid for asylum advice is not tied to the NRM decision making process.

Legal aid for employment law advice

15.156. Potential victims and victims of modern slavery may apply for legal aid in relation to employment law advice for claims under employment law arising in connection with their exploitation.

Legal aid for a civil claim of damages

15.157. Potential victims and victims of modern slavery can apply for legal aid for advice on a claim for damages arising as a result of their being a victim of modern slavery.

Exceptional Case Funding

15.158. An individual requires legal advice but their legal issue is not listed schedule 1, Part 1 of LASP, legal aid may be available via the Exceptional Case Funding (ECF) scheme.

15.159. This could be, for example, for general immigration legal advice or pre-National Referral Mechanism advice in the case of adult potential victims or victims of modern slavery.

Pursuing a civil claim for compensation

15.160. Victims may be able bring a civil claim against a perpetrator where they have suffered damages.

15.161. While being a victim of modern slavery is not its own grounds for compensation, victims can be compensated for a range of damages, such as:

personal injury

losses from theft or damage to property

losses from fraud

being off work

medical expenses

travel expenses

pain and suffering

loss, damage or injury caused to or by a stolen vehicle

15.162. Victims may be able to apply for legal aid to pursue a compensation claim against their exploiter where they meet the relevant legal aid criteria.

Making a claim for publicly funded compensation

15.163. Victims of violent crime are able to apply for compensation under the Criminal Injuries Compensation Scheme (the Scheme). Under the Victims’ Code, victims will be told how to apply for the Scheme by the police when such crimes are reported.

15.164. The Scheme is government funded and exists to compensate victims who suffer serious physical or mental injury as a direct result of a violent crime. The Scheme is for those injured in England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland has its own scheme.

15.165. The rules of the Scheme and the value of the awards paid are approved by Parliament, and the Scheme is administered by the Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority independently of Government, as an Executive Agency of the Ministry of Justice.
